The **Hope Memorial Bridge** (also known as the **Lorain–Carnegie Bridge**) is a 4,490-foot-long (1,370 m)[art deco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_deco "Art deco")[truss bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truss_bridge "Truss bridge") crossing the [Cuyahoga River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuyahoga_River "Cuyahoga River") in [Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland "Cleveland"), Ohio. The bridge connects Lorain Avenue on Cleveland's west side and Carnegie Avenue on the east side, terminating just short of [Progressive Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Field "Progressive Field").

Four pairs of statues designed by sculptor [Henry Hering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Hering "Henry Hering") and architect [Frank Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walker_and_Weeks "Walker and Weeks"), officially named the _**Guardians of Traffic**_,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-3) are sculpted onto opposite-facing ends of two pairs of pylons, a pair at each end of the [viaduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viaduct "Viaduct"). They symbolize progress in transportation.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-4) Each Guardian holds a different vehicle in its hands: a hay wagon, a covered wagon, a stagecoach, and a [1930s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1930s "1930s")-era automobile, as well as four types of motorized trucks used for construction.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-5) The statues are composed of [Berea Sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berea_Sandstone "Berea Sandstone") and were carved in Cleveland's [Little Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_Circle#Little_Italy "University Circle") neighborhood.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-7)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hope_Memorial_Bridge&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Guardian_of_Traffic_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Guardian_of_Traffic_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guardian_of_Traffic_(cropped).jpg)

One of the eight _Guardians of Traffic_

A bond issue to pay for the bridge was passed in 1921, but construction was delayed for years due to squabbles over how the money would be spent. The bridge was completed in 1932 at a cost of $4.75 million ($112,090,000 with inflation[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-inflation-US-8)). It stands 93 feet (28 meters) above the river's waterline in order to allow shipping to pass unobstructed. A second, lower deck designed to carry truck and commercial traffic was never put into service.

The bridge had originally been planned to go through the location of the [Erie Street Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erie_Street_Cemetery "Erie Street Cemetery") on East 9th Street.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-9)

The bridge was listed in the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") on October 8, 1976, after a controversy in which [Cuyahoga County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuyahoga_County,_Ohio "Cuyahoga County, Ohio") engineer [Albert S. Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_S._Porter "Albert S. Porter") threatened to remove the historic pylons to widen the span, stating, "Those columns are monstrosities and should be torn down and forgotten. There is nothing particularly historic about any one of them. We're not running a [May Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Museum_of_Art "Cleveland Museum of Art") here."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-10)

The bridge was renovated in the early 1980s.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-11)

On September 1, 1983, the Lorain–Carnegie bridge was officially renamed the "Hope Memorial Bridge". Press reports vary regarding whom the name honors: William Henry "Harry" Hope, a local [stonemason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonemason "Stonemason") who helped build the _Guardians of Traffic_ sculptures, and the father of comedian and former Cleveland resident Bob Hope;[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-13) Bob Hope himself;[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-14) the entire Hope family;[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-17) or Harry Hope along with the other workers who helped erect the _Guardians of Traffic_.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-18)

On December 10, 2012, officials opened a 14.5-foot-wide (4.4 m) multi-use path on the north side of the bridge, part of a project which also added lighting to the _Guardians of Traffic_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-19)

The inaugural Guardian Mile road race was run across the bridge on August 11, 2018. The elite field boasts multiple Olympians and $14,000 up for grabs in prize money, as well as races for runners of all ages and levels.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-20)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Guardians_of_Traffic_%2851346546565%29.jpg/250px-Guardians_of_Traffic_%2851346546565%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guardians_of_Traffic_(51346546565).jpg)

East end of bridge in relation to [Progressive Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Field "Progressive Field")

On November 19, 2021, the Cleveland Indians of [Major League Baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball "Major League Baseball") changed their name to the [Cleveland Guardians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Guardians "Cleveland Guardians"); the choice was inspired by the _Guardians of Traffic_, which neighbor Progressive Field, the team's home ballpark.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-21)

The **Hope Memorial Bridge** (also known as the **Lorain–Carnegie Bridge**) is a 4,490-foot-long (1,370 m)[art deco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_deco "Art deco")[truss bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truss_bridge "Truss bridge") crossing the [Cuyahoga River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuyahoga_River "Cuyahoga River") in [Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland "Cleveland"), Ohio. The bridge connects Lorain Avenue on Cleveland's west side and Carnegie Avenue on the east side, terminating just short of [Progressive Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Field "Progressive Field").

Four pairs of statues designed by sculptor [Henry Hering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Hering "Henry Hering") and architect [Frank Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walker_and_Weeks "Walker and Weeks"), officially named the _**Guardians of Traffic**_,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-3) are sculpted onto opposite-facing ends of two pairs of pylons, a pair at each end of the [viaduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viaduct "Viaduct"). They symbolize progress in transportation.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-4) Each Guardian holds a different vehicle in its hands: a hay wagon, a covered wagon, a stagecoach, and a [1930s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1930s "1930s")-era automobile, as well as four types of motorized trucks used for construction.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-5) The statues are composed of [Berea Sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berea_Sandstone "Berea Sandstone") and were carved in Cleveland's [Little Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_Circle#Little_Italy "University Circle") neighborhood.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-7)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hope_Memorial_Bridge&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Guardian_of_Traffic_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Guardian_of_Traffic_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guardian_of_Traffic_(cropped).jpg)

One of the eight _Guardians of Traffic_

A bond issue to pay for the bridge was passed in 1921, but construction was delayed for years due to squabbles over how the money would be spent. The bridge was completed in 1932 at a cost of $4.75 million ($112,090,000 with inflation[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-inflation-US-8)). It stands 93 feet (28 meters) above the river's waterline in order to allow shipping to pass unobstructed. A second, lower deck designed to carry truck and commercial traffic was never put into service.

The bridge had originally been planned to go through the location of the [Erie Street Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erie_Street_Cemetery "Erie Street Cemetery") on East 9th Street.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-9)

The bridge was listed in the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") on October 8, 1976, after a controversy in which [Cuyahoga County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuyahoga_County,_Ohio "Cuyahoga County, Ohio") engineer [Albert S. Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_S._Porter "Albert S. Porter") threatened to remove the historic pylons to widen the span, stating, "Those columns are monstrosities and should be torn down and forgotten. There is nothing particularly historic about any one of them. We're not running a [May Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Museum_of_Art "Cleveland Museum of Art") here."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-10)

The bridge was renovated in the early 1980s.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-11)

On September 1, 1983, the Lorain–Carnegie bridge was officially renamed the "Hope Memorial Bridge". Press reports vary regarding whom the name honors: William Henry "Harry" Hope, a local [stonemason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonemason "Stonemason") who helped build the _Guardians of Traffic_ sculptures, and the father of comedian and former Cleveland resident Bob Hope;[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-13) Bob Hope himself;[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-14) the entire Hope family;[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-17) or Harry Hope along with the other workers who helped erect the _Guardians of Traffic_.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-18)

On December 10, 2012, officials opened a 14.5-foot-wide (4.4 m) multi-use path on the north side of the bridge, part of a project which also added lighting to the _Guardians of Traffic_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-19)

The inaugural Guardian Mile road race was run across the bridge on August 11, 2018. The elite field boasts multiple Olympians and $14,000 up for grabs in prize money, as well as races for runners of all ages and levels.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-20)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Guardians_of_Traffic_%2851346546565%29.jpg/250px-Guardians_of_Traffic_%2851346546565%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guardians_of_Traffic_(51346546565).jpg)

East end of bridge in relation to [Progressive Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Field "Progressive Field")

On November 19, 2021, the Cleveland Indians of [Major League Baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball "Major League Baseball") changed their name to the [Cleveland Guardians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Guardians "Cleveland Guardians"); the choice was inspired by the _Guardians of Traffic_, which neighbor Progressive Field, the team's home ballpark.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-21)
